Horvaths rock lizard reaches a hatchling snout–vent length of 2.48 cm [Lb = 2.48 cm], a modest size that reflects the limited yolk reserves available during embryonic development within the parchment-shelled egg. Eggs of this species, measured under controlled laboratory conditions, have an average wet weight of 1.30 grams [Ww0 = 1.30 grams], which sustains the lecithotrophic embryo throughout the entire incubation period. When subjected to an incubation temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the embryonated eggs complete development and hatch after 44 days [ab = 44 days], a duration that is typical for small-bodied lacertids and that ensures the emerging hatchling encounters favourable thermal conditions for its first exogenous feeding.

Upon emergence from the cleidoic egg, the hatchlings of Iberolacerta horvathi display a wet body mass of 0.46 grams [Wwb = 0.46 grams], a value that places them among the lighter offspring within the Iberolacerta clade. This neonatal mass is derived entirely from the depletion of endogenous yolk, with young individuals beginning active feeding only after complete yolk-sac resorption. Growth trajectories during the juvenile phase are strongly temperature-dependent, with puberty in males occurring approximately 3 years after hatching [tp = approximately 3 years after hatching] when lizards are maintained at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The attainment of gonadal activation requires that individuals surpass a critical size threshold; for males, the SVL at puberty has been estimated at 4.50 cm [Lp = 4.50 cm], while females begin reproductive activation at a slightly larger snout–vent length of 4.90 cm [Lp = 4.90 cm].

Adult body size in Horvaths rock lizard shows a moderate degree of sexual dimorphism, with ultimate snout–vent length reaching 6.770 cm [Li = 6.770 cm] in females and 6.165 cm [Li = 6.165 cm] in males based on personal measurements by Dajcman. Correspondingly, the ultimate wet body mass also differs between sexes: females attain a maximum recorded weight of 4.64 grams [Wwi = 4.64 grams], while males, despite their shorter body length, reach a slightly higher adult mass of 4.96 grams [Wwi = 4.96 grams]. This pattern suggests that males invest more heavily in somatic mass relative to skeletal elongation, possibly reflecting divergent selective pressures related to territory defence and male–male combat. These asymptotic sizes are consistent with those reported for other rock-dwelling lacertids inhabiting montane environments in the Dinaric Alps.

Reproductive output in this species is limited by the constraints of a single annual clutch, and females typically lay a single clutch of eggs each year [F_R_i = single clutch of eggs each year], with each clutch containing between 3 and 5 leathery-shelled eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing between 3 and 5 leathery-shelled eggs]. This reproductive strategy, based on estimates from other Iberolacerta species, yields a maximum reproductive rate of 5 eggs per year [Ri = 5 eggs per year] under the thermal regime typical of its high-elevation habitat at 15 °C [T = 15 °C]. The reliance on a single annual clutch reflects the short active season available for gravid individuals to complete egg formation, oviposition, and subsequent incubation before the onset of unfavourable autumn temperatures. Such a slow life-history pace is typical of montane lacertids.

Lifespan data for Iberolacerta horvathi indicate that individuals can survive for up to 9 years [am = up to 9 years] under stable environmental conditions at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], though senescence-related mortality in natural populations likely occurs earlier due to predation and resource limitation. This maximum longevity of 9 years is comparable to that of other small-bodied lacertids that occupy similar cool, rocky habitats. The extended period of reproductive activity, spanning several years after the attainment of puberty, allows females to produce multiple clutches over their lifetime despite the constraint of a single annual reproductive event. Long-term field studies are needed to determine whether post-reproductive mortality or reproductive senescence occurs in this species, but current data suggest a gradual age-related decline in body condition.
